title: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Code Repository
shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Code Repos...
summary: Exfiltration to Code Repository hides stolen data inside ordinary developer traffic. The adversary uses a code hosting service such as GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket as the destination, normally through the service's application programming interface (API) over HTTPS, so the transfer appears as a routine push, commit, gist or release upload. Because engineering teams already authenticate to these services and move large volumes of source code, the channel rarely needs new firewall rules or unusual ports. Artefacts include commits from accounts or tokens that never committed before, repositories created outside working hours, unusually large or binary blobs committed into a repository, personal access tokens used from new addresses or user agents, gist creation by accounts with no development role, and outbound posts to API endpoints with no matching local version control client. Defenders compare repository activity against the person's role and normal tooling, and monitor token creation, scope changes and pushes from hosts that do not run a version control client.

beginner.definition: Exfiltration over a web service means sending stolen data out through a normal internet service. This version uses a code hosting site, where developers keep and share their code. The data is pushed like a normal code update, so it looks ordinary. The traffic is encrypted, so a network monitor sees only that a code site was used.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many companies allow developers to reach code hosting sites, so blocking those sites is not realistic. Attackers use that trust to move files out quietly. A large upload can carry customer lists, keys or source code. If you never look at which accounts push data and at what they push, the theft can continue for months.
howItWorks: The attacker obtains a developer account, a stolen access token, or a new account on a public code service.
They create a private repository, a gist or a release, and they place the collected data inside it.
The data is sent over encrypted HTTPS to the service's API, which is its machine to machine entry point.
Because the same host already talks to that service, network tools see normal developer traffic.
Some attackers split large files into many small commits to stay under size limits or alert rules.
They later download the data from anywhere in the world using the same account or token.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared office where everyone puts letters in one big outgoing tray. A thief does not use the back door. He simply puts his own envelope in the tray with a normal address label, and it leaves with the rest of the post. The mail room trusts the tray rather than each individual sender. Sending stolen files to a code hosting site works the same way, because it leaves through a door that is already open.
takeaways: Treat code hosting traffic as a possible exit path, not only as a development tool.
Watch who creates repositories, tokens and gists, and compare that with the person's role.
Large or unusual files inside a repository deserve a look, even on a private account.

objectives: Explain how a code hosting service can be used as an exfiltration channel.
Describe why HTTPS and popular services give an adversary extra cover.
Identify the repository, token and network artefacts this activity leaves behind.
Explain how to distinguish a developer's normal push activity from suspicious uploads.
Describe monitoring for personal access token creation and unusual scope changes.
